archetypes.name: Simple fact retrieval
archetypes.clues: "What/Who/Where..." with a single stated answer in the text
archetypes.strategy: Scan for the exact detail; quotations are usually accepted
archetypes.traps: Answering with a nearby but wrong detail from the same paragraph

archetypes.name: Multi-item list retrieval
archetypes.clues: "Write down three/four things..."
archetypes.strategy: Read slowly and log each separate item as you meet it - don't stop at the first one or two
archetypes.traps: Missing an item because it's phrased differently to how you'd expect, or merging two items into one

archetypes.name: Ordered list retrieval
archetypes.clues: "...in the order she likes to do them"
archetypes.strategy: Find the exact sequence stated in the text rather than guessing a logical order
archetypes.traps: Getting the items right but the order wrong - order-sensitive marking loses marks even for correct content

archetypes.name: Multiple-select recognition
archetypes.clues: "Tick 4 boxes that accurately match..."
archetypes.strategy: Check each option against the text individually rather than picking the four that 'sound right'
archetypes.traps: Ticking more boxes than instructed loses ALL marks for the question, not just the extra ticks

archetypes.name: Before/after contrast retrieval
archetypes.clues: "What changes after X happens?"
archetypes.strategy: Compare the state of things immediately before and after the pivotal moment
archetypes.traps: Just copying a new detail without explaining that it represents a CHANGE

archetypes.name: Yes/No judgement
archetypes.clues: "Does the author suggest...?" with a tick-box Yes/No
archetypes.strategy: Look at the connotation of the language used (positive/negative words), not just the literal events
archetypes.traps: Answering based on what would be logical rather than what the text's tone actually implies

archetypes.name: Multi-reason justification
archetypes.clues: "Give two/three reasons for your answer"
archetypes.strategy: Pull separate, non-overlapping pieces of evidence - restating the same point in different words doesn't count twice
archetypes.traps: Repeating the same idea in different wording and expecting two marks

archetypes.name: Emotion word inference
archetypes.clues: Euphemistic or indirect phrasing ("this was not a happy moment")
archetypes.strategy: Translate the indirect phrase into a direct, specific emotion word
archetypes.traps: Staying too vague (e.g. 'sad' when 'anxious/guilty' is more precise and required)

archetypes.name: Emotion inference + causal explanation
archetypes.clues: "Why might [character] feel this emotion?"
archetypes.strategy: Link the emotion explicitly to its cause in the plot, not just describe the emotion again
archetypes.traps: Explaining what the emotion IS rather than WHY the character feels it

archetypes.name: Yes/No judgement (ambiguous, evidence-dependent)
archetypes.clues: A genuinely unclear character motivation where either answer can be argued
archetypes.strategy: Pick a side confidently and build a consistent explanation - examiners mark the quality of reasoning, not which side you chose
archetypes.traps: Hedging between both answers instead of committing to one with clear support

archetypes.name: Infer word meaning from context
archetypes.clues: "Explain what you think the word/verb means"
archetypes.strategy: Use surrounding sentences and situation, not a memorised dictionary definition
archetypes.traps: Giving a definition that's technically true but misses the specific connotation the context requires

archetypes.name: Contextual synonym
archetypes.clues: "Write a synonym for [word] (line X)"
archetypes.strategy: Check the word's specific sense in that sentence - many English words have multiple meanings
archetypes.traps: The homonym trap: choosing a correct-sounding synonym for the WRONG sense of the word (e.g. 'grave' meaning solemn vs. a burial site)

archetypes.name: Onomatopoeia/word-choice effect
archetypes.clues: A vivid or unusual verb/adjective highlighted for its sound or feel
archetypes.strategy: Think about how the word sounds or feels physically, not just its dictionary meaning
archetypes.traps: Reading the word's effect as positive when it's actually meant to convey difficulty or unpleasantness

archetypes.name: Atmosphere inference
archetypes.clues: A description of unusual quiet, weather, or setting just before a key event
archetypes.strategy: Connect the atmospheric detail to what it's building towards (tension, unease, significance)
archetypes.traps: Describing WHAT is written (it's quiet) rather than WHY the author included it (to build tension)

archetypes.name: Metaphor implication
archetypes.clues: An unusual descriptive comparison ("the wooden slab of cheese")
archetypes.strategy: Unpack exactly what qualities of the comparison object apply to the real thing being described
archetypes.traps: Stopping at 'it's a metaphor for X' without explaining WHY that comparison is apt

archetypes.name: Extended metaphor/phrase implication
archetypes.clues: A longer, dense phrase blending two ideas ("glittering young adulthood eating cold meat")
archetypes.strategy: Split the phrase into its component images and explain what each contributes before combining them
archetypes.traps: Only explaining half the phrase and missing the contrast it sets up

archetypes.name: Impossibility-to-supernatural inference
archetypes.clues: Something physically impossible is described as happening normally (not feeling a touch that should be felt)
archetypes.strategy: First establish clearly WHY it's impossible under normal physics, then extend to what that impossibility implies
archetypes.traps: Jumping straight to 'it's a ghost' without first explaining the physical impossibility that justifies that leap

archetypes.name: Quotation-explanation triplet
archetypes.clues: "Write down three quotations and explain how each shows..."
archetypes.strategy: Choose three genuinely different pieces of evidence, each with a distinct explanation, rather than three quotes making the same point
archetypes.traps: Paraphrasing instead of quoting exactly (loses the quotation mark); word-for-word accuracy matters even though spelling/punctuation slips are forgiven

archetypes.name: Quotation-explanation pair (character description)
archetypes.clues: A single dense sentence describing a character's appearance/manner, asking for unlikeability or similar
archetypes.strategy: Break the sentence into its separate insults/details and explain the implication of each separately
archetypes.traps: Explaining what the quotation literally says rather than what it implies about character

archetypes.name: Quotation-explanation pair (contrasting emotions)
archetypes.clues: "Write a quotation showing each emotion" where the two emotions may conflict
archetypes.strategy: Actively look for contrast or contradiction between the two required emotions - spotting it is often worth extra credit
archetypes.traps: Choosing two quotations that show the same emotion in different words instead of two distinct emotions

archetypes.name: Character inference from voice alone
archetypes.clues: A character never physically described, known only through speech/dialogue
archetypes.strategy: Work through each line of dialogue in turn, noting both what is said and how (tone, word choice)
archetypes.traps: Confusing which piece of information belongs to which character when there are two speakers

archetypes.name: Comparative character judgement
archetypes.clues: "Which of the two/three characters is most X? Explain."
archetypes.strategy: State your choice explicitly first, then justify with evidence - a bare quotation without explanation only earns partial credit
archetypes.traps: Providing evidence without ever clearly stating an explanation of WHY it supports your choice

archetypes.name: Character relationship analysis
archetypes.clues: "How do X and Y feel about each other?"
archetypes.strategy: Treat it as two separate mini-questions (X's feelings about Y, Y's feelings about X) each needing their own evidence
archetypes.traps: Using evidence that applies to everyone in the scene, not specifically to the relationship being asked about

archetypes.name: Character behaviour inference (either-answer)
archetypes.clues: A question where either interpretation is valid, asking for behaviour evidence rather than a single 'correct' feeling
archetypes.strategy: The same evidence often supports both interpretations - the skill is explaining WHY it supports whichever side was chosen
archetypes.traps: Choosing evidence that doesn't actually fit your stated interpretation

archetypes.name: Subtext inference
archetypes.clues: A character says something generic/indirect that clearly means something more specific in context
archetypes.strategy: Identify the literal meaning first, then explain the additional, more pointed meaning given the situation and tone
archetypes.traps: Only restating the literal words without identifying the underlying message

archetypes.name: Coded-word encoding (position + shift)
archetypes.clues: A worked example showing a word converted into alphabet-position-plus-shift numbers
archetypes.strategy: Find each letter's alphabet position, then calculate the +/- shift to the next letter, following the example format exactly
archetypes.traps: Writing the raw alphabet position of each letter instead of the shift between letters

archetypes.name: Coded-word decoding
archetypes.clues: A full code given, asking which word it represents
archetypes.strategy: Apply each shift in turn starting from the first letter's position, converting each result back to a letter
archetypes.traps: Losing track when a shift takes the count past Z (wrapping) or below A

archetypes.name: Coded-word reverse-deduction (partial code)
archetypes.clues: Part of the code is blank; the word must be deduced from the letters you CAN decode
archetypes.strategy: Decode what you can first to get a partial word, guess the only sensible word that completes it, then calculate the missing shift
archetypes.traps: Guessing a plausible word without checking it's consistent with every other given digit in the code

archetypes.name: Reversed shared-letter-pair completion
archetypes.clues: Two words share a missing letter-pair, with the pair reversed in the second word
archetypes.strategy: Solve the first word's gap, then test the pair in reverse order against the second word's gap positions
archetypes.traps: Forgetting to reverse the pair for the second word

archetypes.name: Same-order shared-letter-pair completion
archetypes.clues: Two words share a missing letter-pair in the SAME order in both
archetypes.strategy: Solve one word's gap, then test that exact pair (not reversed) against the other word
archetypes.traps: Applying the reversal rule from a different question type by mistake

archetypes.name: Shared-letter-pair completion (same order, synonym pair)
archetypes.clues: Two words with a similar MEANING share a missing letter-pair or set of letters, same order
archetypes.strategy: Use the synonym relationship to guess the whole word first, then verify the shared letters fit both gap patterns
archetypes.traps: Focusing only on the letter pattern and ignoring the meaning clue, which usually narrows things down faster

thinking_skills.name: Automatic Recall
thinking_skills.description: Direct retrieval of a fact, word meaning, or quotation that's stated plainly in the text.

thinking_skills.name: Application
thinking_skills.description: Using textual evidence and context to support a judgement, inference, or explanation.

thinking_skills.name: Multi-stage Planning
thinking_skills.description: Combining several separate pieces of evidence or explanation in a structured way, often across multiple marks.

thinking_skills.name: Pattern Recognition
thinking_skills.description: Spotting a recurring structure (a code, a letter pattern) and applying it consistently.

thinking_skills.name: Reverse Reasoning
thinking_skills.description: Working backwards from a coded or partial result to the original word or meaning.

thinking_skills.name: Logical Deduction
thinking_skills.description: Reasoning through evidence systematically to reach and justify a conclusion, especially where the text is ambiguous.

importance_tiers.name: Must Get
importance_tiers.description: Direct retrieval or clear-cut Yes/No judgements. Appears almost every year in a similar form - missing these is a red flag.

importance_tiers.name: Should Get
importance_tiers.description: Requires combining two or three pieces of evidence, but the evidence itself is easy to locate.

importance_tiers.name: Strong Candidate
importance_tiers.description: Requires genuine inference beyond the literal text - tone, implication, or character motivation.

importance_tiers.name: Separator
importance_tiers.description: Multi-mark quotation-and-explanation questions, ambiguous-answer character judgements, or dense figurative language - these differentiate top scorers.
